title: Welcome Back: What Did You Keep?
goal: I can show what I remember: fact shortcuts, the area model, division facts and leftovers.

card.desc: Welcome-back review after the three-week break. Bailey opens by presenting her Gratitude Project poster, then shows what she kept from Weeks 1–4: the four fact shortcuts, the area model, division facts and fact families, and remainders. No new skill; this lesson finds what slipped before long division starts on Monday. Seven new words, including retain and resilient.

win: You kept your tools sharp over the break. You are ready for long division!

slides.title: Welcome Back: What Did You Keep?
slides.text: Welcome back! First, you present your Gratitude Project poster. Then we find out which math tools you kept over the break: fact shortcuts, the area model and division.

notes.do: Have ready: her Gratitude Project poster and worksheet pages 3 and 4, about 50 dried beans, 6 cups or paper plates, whiteboard and marker, and her book. Prop the poster where she can stand beside it.
notes.say: "Welcome back! Today is not about anything new. I want to see what you kept. If something slipped, that is normal after three weeks, and we fix it today."
notes.ask: "Did you finish the Lesson 11 work over the break? Which part felt easy and which part felt hard?"

slides.title: Present your poster
slides.text: Stand next to your poster. Talk to your audience, not to the poster.
prompts: Read your title. Then tell what the project was and who was in it.
Show your bar graph. Which topic had the most slips? What does that tell you about your family?
Read your Gratitude Report paragraph. Point to your main idea sentence.
Share your 3 favorite quotes. Which one means the most to you, and why?
starters: Our family filled a Gratitude Jar for …
The topic with the most slips was …, which tells me …

notes.do: 8 minutes. She presents for about 5 minutes; you listen without interrupting. Then ask two questions. Press the gold button for each strong answer.
notes.say: When she finishes: "Thank you. Tell me one thing you did really well, and one thing you would change next time."
notes.ask: "How did you make the bar graph from the tally marks?" "Which Word Bank words did you use in your paragraph?"
notes.listen: Eye contact, a clear main idea sentence, and a detail from the graph used as evidence. Praise one specific thing out loud ("You looked up at me when you read your main idea").

slides.title: Back to Berk
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: Where are you in the book now? Tell the most important thing that happened since Lesson 11.
How has Hiccup changed since the beginning of the book? Give one event as proof.
Which character would you like to ask a question? What would you ask?
starters: Since Lesson 11, the most important thing was …
At first Hiccup …, but now he …

notes.do: 6 minutes. Let her hold the book and find pages.
notes.ask: "How has Hiccup changed? Prove it with one thing he did."
notes.listen: A change (from scared or unsure to braver or more confident) backed by a real event. If she only retells, ask: "So what is different about him now?"

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read it out loud. Then use it in your own sentence about the break or about math.

words.meaning: Objects set out in equal rows and columns.
words.example: An array with 7 rows of 8 shields shows 7 × 8 = 56.

words.meaning: Able to do something quickly, easily and correctly.
words.example: When you are fluent with 9 × 8, you know it is 72 without adding.

words.meaning: To keep something, like keeping a fact in your memory.
words.example: Did you retain your fact shortcuts over the break?

words.meaning: To go back to something and look at it again.
words.example: Today we revisit the area model before we learn long division.

words.meaning: To think carefully about something that happened.
words.example: The Gratitude Project helped me reflect on what my family means to me.

words.meaning: Able to bounce back and keep going after something goes wrong.
words.example: A resilient learner tries a hard problem again instead of quitting.

words.meaning: A long story about heroes and their adventures, like the old stories about the Vikings.
words.example: Hiccup's adventures with Toothless feel like a Viking saga.

notes.do: She reads each card and makes her own sentence. Write retain and fluent on the whiteboard; you will use them all lesson.
notes.say: "Two math words, array and fluent, and five story words. Saga is a Viking word, so it belongs with your book."
notes.ask: "What is one thing you retained from the Gratitude Project?" "Is a resilient person someone who never fails? Why not?"
notes.listen: For resilient: she should say a resilient person DOES fail or struggle but keeps going. For fluent: quick AND correct.

slides.title: Four fact shortcuts
slides.text: When a fact is not automatic yet, do not add the number over and over. Use a shortcut.

steps.text: ×8 = double, double, double. 8 × 9: 9 doubled is 18, doubled again is 36, doubled again is 72.

slides.tip: Pick the shortcut that matches the 6, 7, 8 or 9 in the fact.

notes.do: Before each step, cover the answer and ask her to say the shortcut first. Write each one on the whiteboard as she says it.
notes.say: After each correct step: "Yes! You retained that one."
notes.ask: "Which shortcut would you use for 9 × 6?" before you reveal Step 1, and the same for each step.
notes.listen: She names the shortcut, not just the answer. If she starts adding 9 + 9 + 9 …, stop her kindly: "That works, but it is the slow road. Which shortcut fits a 9?"

slides.title: Which shortcut?
slides.text: Say the shortcut out loud first. Then type the answer.

items.no: Use ×10 minus one group: 10 × 8 = 80. Now take away one 8.

items.why: Double 8 is 16, double again is 32, double again is 64.
items.no: Double 8, then double again, then double again.

notes.do: She types each answer herself. Count silently: under 3 seconds means fluent.
notes.say: Praise each one right away: "Fluent!" or "Right, and you used the shortcut."
notes.listen: Which facts are slow. Write them on an index card for her to keep; they go on her task list as extra practice.

slides.title: The area model
slides.text: For a 2-digit number times a 1-digit number, break the big number into tens and ones. Multiply each part. Add.

steps.text: Estimate first. 68 × 7: 68 is close to 70. 70 × 7 = 490, so the answer is about 490.
Break it apart. 68 = 60 + 8. Make one box for 60 and one box for 8.
Multiply each box. 60 × 7 = 420 and 8 × 7 = 56.
Add. 420 + 56 = 476. That is close to 490, so it makes sense.

slides.tip: Adding 7 sixty-eight times would take forever. Two boxes take one minute.

notes.do: Draw the two boxes on the whiteboard while she watches, then let her fill in the numbers.
notes.ask: "Why 60 and not 6?" (The 6 is in the tens place, so it is 60.) "Why do we estimate first?" (To know if the answer makes sense.)
notes.listen: The classic slip is 6 × 7 = 42 instead of 60 × 7 = 420. If she says 42, point to the tens place.

slides.title: Area model and the smart method

items.q: Hiccup needs 38 × 9. Which way is the most efficient and correct?
choices: Count by 9s until you get to 38
items.why: The area model keeps the place value: 270 + 72 = 342.
no: That works, but it is slow, and it is easy to lose track.
The 3 is in the tens place. It means 30, not 3.
Counting to 38 by 9s does not answer 38 × 9.

notes.do: She draws the 84 × 6 boxes on the whiteboard before she types.
notes.ask: On the Hiccup item: "What is wrong with 27 + 72?" (It treats 30 like 3.)
notes.listen: She explains why the area model wins: it is fast AND keeps the tens as tens.

slides.title: Division undoes multiplication
slides.text: Every division fact asks a multiplication question. 63 ÷ 7 means 7 × ? = 63. 7 × 9 = 63, so 63 ÷ 7 = 9.

steps.text: A fact family uses the same three numbers. For 6, 8 and 48: 6 × 8 = 48 and 8 × 6 = 48.
The two division facts start with the biggest number: 48 ÷ 6 = 8 and 48 ÷ 8 = 6.

slides.tip: Division question? Say the multiplication question first.

notes.do: Point to the triangle: biggest number on top.
notes.ask: "What does 54 ÷ 9 ask?" (9 × ? = 54.) "Say all four facts for 6, 8 and 48."
notes.listen: Division facts that start with the biggest number. If she says "6 ÷ 48", ask: "Can you share 6 beans among 48 plates?"

items.why: The biggest number is missing, so multiply: 7 × 6 = 42.
items.no: The biggest number is missing. Multiply 7 × 6.

items.q: Which fact is not in the fact family for 7, 9 and 63?
items.why: A division fact in this family starts with 63, the biggest number. 7 ÷ 63 is backward.
no: That one is in the family: 9 × 7 = 63.
That one is in the family.
That one is in the family: 7 × 9 = 63.

notes.ask: For each: "Which number is missing: the biggest one or a smaller one? Do you multiply or divide?"
notes.listen: "The biggest is missing, so I multiply." Praise that sentence every time she says it.

slides.title: Feeding time on Berk
slides.text: Stoick shares 48 fish equally among 6 dragons. Use the buttons to show the dragons and the fish each one gets.
slides.hint: The number of groups is the number of dragons. Then ask: 6 × what = 48?

notes.do: First she predicts with a fact (6 × ? = 48). Then she deals 48 beans onto 6 plates to prove it. Then she sets the buttons.
notes.ask: "Prediction first: 6 times what is 48?" After the beans: "Did your fact match the plates?"
notes.listen: "6 × 8 = 48, so 8 each." If she counts the beans one by one, let her finish, then ask which fact would have told her faster.

slides.title: Leftovers
slides.text: Sometimes things do not share evenly. The amount left over is the remainder.

steps.text: 50 ÷ 8. Find the biggest 8s fact that is not more than 50: 8 × 6 = 48. (8 × 7 = 56 is too big.)
Subtract: 50 − 48 = 2. Two are left over.
That makes 6 full groups of 8, and a small pile of 2 is left over. So 50 ÷ 8 = 6 R 2.
The remainder must be smaller than the divisor. 2 is smaller than 8, so the answer is right.

slides.tip: If the remainder is as big as the divisor or bigger, another group fits.

notes.do: Hands-on: she deals 50 beans into piles of 8 and shows the 2 left in her hand.
notes.ask: "Why can't the remainder be 10?" (Then another pile of 8 would fit.)
notes.listen: "The remainder has to be smaller than what I divide by." This rule is the bridge to next week's long division.

items.no: Find the biggest 6s fact that is not more than 47.

items.q: Fishlegs says 60 ÷ 7 = 7 R 11. What is wrong?
choices: 11 is bigger than 7, so another 7 fits: it is 8 R 4.
no: A remainder of 11 is bigger than the divisor 7. Another group fits.
7 × 9 = 63. That is more than 60.
18 is even bigger than 7. Two more groups fit.

notes.do: Beans ready for any item she is unsure of.
notes.ask: On the Fishlegs item: "How could Fishlegs catch his own mistake?" (11 is bigger than 7.)
notes.listen: She checks the remainder against the divisor without being asked. Praise it: "That check is exactly what you will need next week."

items.q: Over the break, Bailey still knew every ×9 fact. She retained them. What does that mean?
choices: She kept them in her memory.
items.why: To retain is to keep something, like keeping facts in your memory.
no: Forgetting is the opposite of retaining.
Writing is not the same as remembering.
Teaching is not what retain means. (And River is a dog!)

items.q: Toothless can answer 8 × 7 = 56 in one second, every time. He is ____ with that fact. (Use a word from your word cards.)
Which is the best example of a saga?
choices: a long story about a Viking hero's adventures
items.why: A saga is a long story about heroes and their adventures.
no: A list is not a story.
A times table is math, not a story.
A saga is long, and it is about heroes.

notes.ask: "Use resilient in a sentence about something hard you did this year."
notes.listen: She uses the word with a real example from her own life.

slides.title: Show me before you go
slides.text: On your own. No help this time.

items.no: Find the biggest 7s fact that is not more than 45.

notes.do: She types these herself. Write down any miss: that is the skill to warm up with on Monday.
notes.listen: All three right means the review stuck. Tell her so.

slides.title: What is next
slides.text: You kept a lot over the break! Next week is something new: long division. You will use your facts, your subtracting and your remainder rule.

steps.text: Tonight: the After-class lesson. It ends with Show What You Know. You need 90.
This weekend: the Lesson 12 Practice, the Lesson 12 Packet, a reading lesson, and 15 minutes of reading each day.
Monday on Zoom: Lesson 13, your first long division lesson.

slides.tip: Keep your index card of slow facts. Quiz yourself for one minute a day.

notes.do: Open the course page and go through the Lesson 12 task list with her (and with Tia if she is there).
notes.say: "You were resilient today. Long division looks big, but it is just your facts, one step at a time."
notes.ask: "Which of the four shortcuts do you want to practice most this weekend?"

slides.title: On Your Own: Welcome Back!
slides.text: In class you presented your poster and showed what you kept from before the break. Now you review on your own. It takes about 25 minutes and ends with Show What You Know.

slides.title: Teach it to someone
slides.text: Find someone at home. Say each answer out loud before you go on.
prompts: Teach them the ×9 shortcut with 9 × 7. Then the ×6 shortcut with 6 × 8.
Tell them what you reflected on while you made your Gratitude poster.
Tell them about a moment in How to Train Your Dragon when a character was resilient.
starters: While I made my poster, I reflected on …

slides.title: Your math toolbox
slides.text: Tap Show me the next step to see each tool.

steps.text: ×9 = ×10 minus one group  ·  ×6 = ×5 plus one group  ·  ×8 = double, double, double  ·  ×7 = ×5 plus ×2
Division: 56 ÷ 8 asks 8 × ? = 56. The answer is 7.
Leftovers: 22 ÷ 4 = 5 R 2, because 4 × 5 = 20 and 2 are left. The remainder is smaller than the divisor.

slides.tip: Never add the same number over and over. Pick a tool.

items.no: Double 6, then double again, then double again.

items.why: ×6 = ×5 plus one group: 5 × 9 = 45, plus one more 9 is 54.
no: The ×9 shortcut takes away one group of 6, not 9: 60 − 6 = 54.
That adds instead of multiplying.
The extra group is one more 9, not one more 6.

items.q: Which shows the area model for 46 × 7?
no: The 4 is in the tens place. It means 40.
That adds instead of multiplying.
The 6 must be multiplied by 7 too.

slides.title: Fact or area model?
slides.text: Tap a problem. Then tap the box with the most efficient way to solve it.

items.why: Both numbers are single digits. It is one fact: 72.

items.hint: Does one number have tens and ones?
Does one number have tens and ones?
Does one number have tens and ones?

slides.done: Single digits: use a fact. Tens and ones: use the area model.

items.why: The biggest number is missing, so multiply: 8 × 8 = 64.
items.no: The biggest number is missing. Multiply.

items.q: Three facts in a family: 7 × 6 = 42, 6 × 7 = 42, 42 ÷ 7 = 6. What is the missing division fact? Type it.
items.no: Start with 42, the biggest number. Divide by 6.
Find the biggest 6s fact that is not more than 38.

items.q: Stoick has 45 fish for 6 dragons. Each dragon gets the same number. How many fish does each dragon get, and how many are left?
no: 6 × 8 = 48. That is more fish than Stoick has.
9 left is more than 6. Each dragon can get one more.
Check the subtraction: 45 − 42 = 3.

items.q: To keep facts in your memory is to ____ them. (Use a word from your word cards.)
items.no: It starts with r and ends with -ain.

items.q: Objects set out in equal rows and columns make an ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
items.why: An array has equal rows and columns.

items.q: Hiccup's plan failed, but he tried again the next day. Which word describes him?

no: Fluent means quick and correct, not bouncing back.
Retained means kept in memory.
Revisit means go back and look again.
×10 minus one group only works for ×9.
The 2 must be 2 × 6 = 12, not just 2.
That adds instead of multiplying.

sets.q: Which is the most efficient way to find 47 × 6?
no: That works, but it is slow and easy to lose track.
The 4 is in the tens place. It means 40.
Counting to 47 does not find 47 × 6.
10 is bigger than 8. Another group fits.
8 × 8 = 64. That is more than 58.
Check the subtraction: 58 − 56 = 2.

sets.q: Able to do something quickly, easily and correctly is ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
Before the test, Hiccup wants to revisit his notes about dragons. What will he do?
sets.why: To revisit is to go back and look at something again.
no: That is the opposite of revisiting.
Revisiting means going back to what is already there.
Hiding them does not mean looking at them again.
That is only 3 sevens, and it is adding.
×10 minus one group works for ×9, not ×8.
×7 = ×5 plus ×2. You need 2 × 8 = 16, not 7.

sets.q: Which problem is best solved with just a fact?
sets.why: 9 × 6 is one fact: 54. The others have tens and ones, so they need the area model.
no: 93 has tens and ones. Use the area model.
36 has tens and ones. Use the area model.
69 has tens and ones. Use the area model.

sets.why: The biggest number is missing, so multiply: 7 × 9 = 63.
sets.no: The biggest number is missing. Multiply.

no: 10 is bigger than 6. Another group fits.
6 × 6 = 36. That is more than 34.
Check the subtraction: 34 − 30 = 4.

sets.q: To think carefully about something that happened is to ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
sets.why: To reflect is to think carefully about something that happened.
sets.no: It starts with r and ends with -ect.

sets.q: Which is the best example of an array?
choices: 5 rows of chairs with 6 chairs in every row
6 chairs in a line and 4 chairs in a circle
sets.why: An array has equal rows and columns: 5 rows of 6.
no: A pile has no rows or columns.
The rows are not equal.
One chair is not rows and columns.
Ten 8s is 80, not 90.
That adds instead of multiplying.
Take away one group of 8, not 9.

sets.q: Snotlout found 34 × 7 like this: 3 × 7 + 4 × 7 = 21 + 28 = 49. What went wrong?
choices: The 3 means 30, so the first box is 30 × 7 = 210.
no: 49 is far too small. 34 × 7 is more than 30 × 7 = 210.
That adds instead of multiplying.
The order of the boxes does not matter.

sets.q: Toothless has 30 fish. He eats 4 a day. How many full days will the fish last, and how many fish are left?
no: 4 × 8 = 32. That is more fish than he has.
6 left is more than 4. There is enough for another day.
Check the subtraction: 30 − 28 = 2.

A worksheet is not a story.
A weather report is not a story about heroes.

teacher.objective: Bailey presents her Gratitude Project poster, then shows what she retained from Weeks 1–4: the four 6–9 fact shortcuts (×9 = ×10 − one group, ×6 = ×5 + one group, ×8 = double, double, double, ×7 = ×5 + ×2), choosing a fact or the area model, the area model for 2-digit × 1-digit, division facts and fact families, and small remainders that must be smaller than the divisor. No new skill.
materials: Class lesson on your laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Her Gratitude Project poster and worksheet pages 3 and 4
About 50 dried beans or counters and 6 cups or paper plates
One index card for her slow facts
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): done at home this weekend

plan.do: Class slide 1. Poster propped up, beans, cups, whiteboard. Ask how the Lesson 11 break work went.
Class slide 2. She presents (about 5 minutes): title, bar graph, paragraph, 3 quotes. You ask two questions and praise one specific thing.
Class slide 3. Where she is in the book, how Hiccup has changed, with an event as proof.
Class slide 4. She reads each card and makes her own sentence. Retain and fluent on the whiteboard.
Class slides 5–6. She says each shortcut before you reveal it, then four facts; note slow facts on an index card.
Class slides 7–8. Estimate, two boxes, add (68 × 7); then 84 × 6 on the whiteboard and the efficient-method question.
Class slides 9–11. Multiplication question first, fact families, then 48 beans onto 6 plates to prove 48 ÷ 6 = 8.
Class slides 12–13. 50 beans in piles of 8 (6 R 2); remainder smaller than the divisor; Fishlegs' 7 R 11 mistake.
Class slide 14. Retain, fluent, saga in context; resilient in her own sentence.
Class slide 15. Three items on her own. Note any miss for Monday's warm-up.
Class slide 16. Preview long division; open the course page and go through the Lesson 12 task list.

watch: Adding the same number over and over (9 + 9 + 9 …) when a fact is slow. Stop her kindly and ask: "Which shortcut fits a 9?"
On the ×9 shortcut, taking away the wrong group (6 × 9 = 60 − 9 = 51). Ask: "Ten groups of what? Then take away one group of that."
In the area model, treating the tens digit as ones (3 × 7 instead of 30 × 7). Point to the tens place and ask what the digit is worth.
Writing division facts backward (6 ÷ 48). Ask: "Can you share 6 beans among 48 plates?"
A remainder as big as or bigger than the divisor (60 ÷ 7 = 7 R 11). Ask: "Could another group fit?"
"I can't do it" after the break. Say: "You did this before the break. What is the first step?" Then praise the first step out loud before she does the next.

packet_key.answer: array → equal rows and columns; fluent → quick, easy and correct; retain → to keep in your memory; revisit → to go back and look again; reflect → to think carefully about what happened; resilient → bounces back and keeps going; saga → a long story about heroes
44 ÷ 6 = 7 R 2: 7 dragons get 6 fish, 2 fish are left (6 × 7 = 42)
No. The remainder 9 is bigger than the divisor 5, so another group fits. 39 ÷ 5 = 7 R 4 (5 × 7 = 35, 39 − 35 = 4).
Answers vary; complete sentences, uses reflect correctly, names something real from the project.
Answers vary; a real moment from the book where a character bounces back after something goes wrong, with resilient used correctly.

teacher.notes: Bailey takes Show What You Know on her own tonight at the end of the After-class lesson. Check her Formspree score and the exit ticket before Monday. If she scores under 90, look at which part slipped (shortcuts, area model, division facts or remainders): on Monday, spend the warm-up on that one part, and she retakes Show What You Know (a brand-new question set). Long division on Monday depends most on division facts and the remainder rule, so reteach those first if both slipped.

Sunday: do the reading lesson Reading Power: Nonfiction Ninja. Read short nonfiction passages and answer questions about what you learned. Aim for 90. If it is locked, type 1111.
Friday, Saturday and Sunday: read How to Train Your Dragon for 15 minutes each day. Find a moment when a character is resilient.
